items.note: Nagpur inscription belongs to Naravarman, son of Udayaditya, who became the next Paramara king in 1094 and ruled to 1133; it gives the dynasty's succession up to him and was composed by Naravarman himself (verse 56).
items.gloss: The Nagpur inscription is of King Naravarman, son of King Udayaditya, who became the next king of the Paramara dynasty in 1094 after Udayaditya and ruled until 1133 CE. It has full information on the Paramara dynasty up to Naravarman, who succeeded whom. Verse 56 makes clear that this prashasti was composed by King Naravarman himself.

items.note: Jainad inscription of Udayaditya's youngest son Jagadeva (verse 6) calls Udayaditya his father and Bhojaraja his paternal uncle (pitrivya).
items.gloss: In verse 6 of the Jainad inscription of Jagadeva, Udayaditya's youngest son: 'He whose father was Udayaditya and whose uncle (pitrivya) was the divine Bhojaraja.' It means: 'Whose father was Udayaditya, and the god Bhojaraja was the paternal uncle; these two, growing brilliant, attained sovereignty over the earth by their own splendour and were established.'

claim.value: Bhoja was paternal uncle (pitrivya) - Jainad inscription v.6 of Jagadeva

items.note: Dongargaon inscription (v.5) of Jagadeva calls Udayaditya Bhoja's brother (bhrata), while the Jainad inscription of the same writer calls Bhoja his father's uncle.
items.gloss: Meaning: 'After him (Bhojadeva), his brother Udayaditya grew in power, who rescued the Malwa land, which had been (reduced to dust) by the attack of three enemies.' In the Jainad inscription Jagadeva wrote King Udayaditya as his father and King Bhojadeva as uncle (pitrivya), whereas in the Dongargaon inscription Jagadeva writes his father Udayaditya as Bhojadeva's 'brother'.

items.note: Genealogy per Jagadeva's records: Jagadeva was the third and youngest son; the elder were Lakshmadeva (died in his father's time) and Naravarman (next ruler).
items.gloss: Jagadeva was the third and youngest prince of his father Udayaditya (as his inscriptions say). Two elder brothers were Lakshmadeva and Naravarman. Prince Lakshmadeva did not survive in his father's time. Prince Naravarman became the next ruler of the Paramaras after Udayaditya's death.

items.note: Chronological puzzle: if Bhoja and Udayaditya were brothers, Udayaditya should have become king after Bhoja's death in 1055, yet he waited until 1070; Bhoja appears at Dhar in 1011.
items.gloss: The exact date of King Sindhuraja's death is not known, but his son King Bhojadeva appears as a king at Dhar in 1011 CE. If they were brothers, Udayaditya should normally have become king after Bhojadeva's death in 1055 CE. Why did he have to wait until 1070 CE?

claim.value: accession c. 1070 CE, Bhoja died 1055 (as stated by this author)

items.note: Argument that if Udayaditya were Bhoja's kinsman he should be mentioned in some inscription or book of Bhoja's time.
items.gloss: One argument is also that if he had been Bhoja's kinsman, he should have been mentioned somewhere in some inscription or book of Bhoja's time.

items.note: Historiography on the Udayaditya-Bhoja relation as summarised by Verma: Kielhorn (position not restated in this chunk) and D. C. Ganguly, who cites an Ain-i-Akbari account in favour of the same conclusion.
items.gloss: Here comes the name of Professor Franz Kielhorn, who held the same view. Then there is mention of D. C. Ganguly on this question, who brings an account from the Ain-i-Akbari in favour of the same conclusion.

items.note: H. C. Ray, in Dynastic History of Northern India, opposed Ganguly's view and does not take 'bandhu' to mean brother.
items.gloss: Ganguly's view was opposed by H. C. Ray in his book 'Dynastic History of Northern India'. He does not take bandhu to mean brother.

claim.value: H. C. Ray: 'bandhu' does not mean brother

refs: H. C. Ray, Dynastic History of Northern India

items.note: Author's recommendation that each new discovery be explained to local people in simple language, books updated, and university history departments and archaeology departments made dynamic.
items.gloss: But in matters of history our interest should be how to explain things to local people in very simple language, how to update books with every new discovery, and most importantly how to make stagnant minds in the jobs of university history departments and the culture and archaeology department dynamic.

items.note: Author's view of destroyed centres (Nalanda, Vikramashila, Vijayanagara) and of the Vijay temple at Vidisha, built by Naravarman, as the most painful example of lost inscriptions.
items.gloss: Go to Nalanda and Vikramashila in Bihar, to Vijayanagara far off in Karnataka. Much lies scattered in every corner of the country to mourn. We do not know how many valuable inscriptions there were in these developed settlements before destruction, which were badly erased and turned to stone dust. In Vidisha itself the Vijay temple built by Naravarman is the most painful example of this.

items.note: Verma asks who actually built Udaypur; an undated, more than half-illegible inscription of Udayaditya's time gives valuable clues about the town and the temple.
items.gloss: Verma brings the next question: who actually built Udaypur? An inscription of Udayaditya's time (later than the Udaypur prashasti but undated) gives some valuable clues about this. But more than half of it has become unreadable because of heavy damage. It has no date either. Perhaps it was in the part that was destroyed. Its importance is that it gives clues about the town of Udaypur and the temple.

claim.value: undated Udayaditya-period inscription gives clues; half illegible (Verma)

items.note: Inscription found in a house in Chatua Darwaza mohalla, not the temple precinct; now in the Gwalior archaeological museum; 27 lines, Sanskrit.
items.gloss: This inscription was obtained not in the temple complex of Udaypur but from a house in the Chatua Darwaza locality. This precious piece of stone is today in the Gwalior archaeological museum. It has 27 lines in all. Like the Udaypur prashasti its language is Sanskrit.

items.note: Entirely in verse; badly worn, little could be read, but it gives a glimpse of Udaypur's past; cited as Annual Report of the Archaeological Department in Gwalior State 1925-26, no. 71, pp. 12-13.
items.gloss: It is entirely in verse. The stone is much worn. Only very little could be read. Whatever was read shows a splendid glimpse of Udaypur's past. It is mentioned in the Annual Report of the Archaeological Department in Gwalior State 1925-26, no. 71, pages 12-13.
refs: Annual Report of the Archaeological Department, Gwalior State, 1925-26, no. 71, pp. 12-13

items.note: Lines 1-6 describe Udayaditya's military victories; the only named one is the Chedi ruler 'Dhahaladhisha', defeated and killed; Dhahala is around Jabalpur, thought the Kalachuri homeland.
items.gloss: Lines one to six describe some important military victories of Udayaditya. Among these conquered the name only of the Chedi ruler of Dhahala-mandala, the 'Dhahaladhisha', is given. It is recorded in the inscription that the Dhahaladhisha was defeated and killed. Dhahala was originally the area around Jabalpur, which is considered the original home of the Kalachuris.

items.note: Argues the name itself shows Udaypur is connected with Udayaditya; absence of earlier Paramara records shows the town came into existence in his time.
items.gloss: As far as Udaypur is concerned, its very name shows it is related to King Udayaditya. That no inscription of earlier Paramara kings is found here shows that this town came into existence in Udayaditya's time.

claim.value: founded in Udayaditya's time; named after him; no earlier Paramara records here

items.note: In Vidisha district, Jayasimha is probably the first Paramara ruler whose record is found here; the genealogy goes only up to Udayadityadeva.
items.gloss: In Vidisha district Jayasimha is probably the first Paramara ruler whose inscription is found here. In this too the genealogy of Paramara kings goes only up to Udayadityadeva.

items.note: Later lines mention local rulers of the Nemaka lineage under the Paramaras; possibly Udayaditya gave the area to a Nemaka feudatory; the rest unreadable.
items.gloss: In the later lines of this inscription there is an account of local rulers of a Nemaka dynasty under the Paramaras. Since Udaypur was under direct Paramara rule, how could another dynasty be mentioned? It is possible that King Udayaditya had assigned this area to a feudatory of the Nemaka lineage. Perhaps this incomplete inscription had more details about the Nemakas, but they have not survived to be read.

items.note: Per the inscription, the unnamed son of the feudatory Shudraka (Nemaka lineage, Shiva worshippers) built a temple at Udaypur; the author conjectures this family were local administrators when construction began.
items.gloss: This inscription tells that the Nemaka-line rulers were worshippers of Shiva. Another feudatory named Shudraka defeated some Gurjara king. The inscription describes that the son of this Shudraka, whose name is unclear, had a temple built at Udaypur. We can only guess that when construction of the Udaypur temple began, this feudatory family of the Nemaka line may have been the local administrator here and the temple was built under its supervision.

claim.value: unnamed son of feudatory Shudraka (Nemaka line), per this inscription (author's reading)

items.note: Paramara patronage of learning and monuments; knowledge centres at Ujjain, Dhara, Mandu, Bhojpal, Vidisha and Udaypur.
items.gloss: We know well that the fame of ambitious Paramara kings is not only for valour and conquests. In their time all branches of knowledge found shelter. Unmatched monuments of architecture were built for centuries. Around these monuments big knowledge centres arose up to Ujjain, Dhara, Mandu, Bhojpal, Vidisha and Udaypur, which these kings raised to heights.

items.note: Udaypur prashasti: the most important source on the Paramara dynasty from its origin to Udayaditya; fragmentary; found in the Nilakantheshwar temple courtyard; kept in Gwalior museum; Sanskrit, 11th-century Nagari.
items.gloss: The most important source of information on the Paramara dynasty is the 'Udaypur prashasti'. It presents an account of their achievements from the origin of the Paramara dynasty to King Udayaditya. This inscription is damaged. Found in the courtyard of the Nilakanteshwar temple of Udaypur, this stone is the most important testimony of Udaypur's history. This most precious stone of Udaypur is kept in the Gwalior museum. Its language is Sanskrit and the script is 11th-century Nagari.

claim.value: found in Nilakantheshwar temple courtyard; now Gwalior museum; damaged; undated

items.note: The prashasti bears no date but appears from its content to be of Udayaditya's time; his reign is given as 1070 to 1093.
items.gloss: No date is marked on it but according to information from this inscription it appears to be of the time of King Udayaditya, successor of King Bhoja. King Udayaditya's reign was between 1070 and 1093.

items.note: Names other documents of the era: Padmagupta's Navasahasankacharita and Merutunga's Prabandhachintamani.
items.gloss: Such as the documents of that era like Padmagupta's Navasahasankacharita and Merutunga's Prabandhachintamani.

items.note: Background: political change after the 8th-century tripartite struggle of Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta; new dynasties emerged, notably the Chalukyas of Kalyani.
items.gloss: After the tripartite struggle among the Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta dynasties in the eighth century, there were big political changes in north and south India. Some new dynasties emerged and recorded their splendid presence in history. Most notable among them in the south were the Chalukyas of Kalyani, successors of the Chalukya dynasty of Vatapi.

items.note: With the Pratihara decline three powers rose together: Chedi of the Kalachuris, Chandellas of Jejakabhukti and Paramaras of Malwa.
items.gloss: When the Pratiharas' strength weakened, three powers emerged. Among them the Chedis of the Kalachuris, the Chandellas of Jejakabhukti and the Paramaras of Malwa rise on the horizon together.

items.note: Extent of the Paramara realm: Malwa, Bhopal, Vidisha and Udaypur, Hansol, Modasa, Mahudi; Hoshangabad on the Narmada to Kota.
items.gloss: In their long period of five centuries ambitious Paramara kings expanded their borders over a large area. Their kingdom spread with Malwa beyond Bhopal to Vidisha and Udaypur, in the west to areas like Hansol, Modasa and Mahudi. Paramaras ruled areas from Hoshangabad on the Narmada coast in the south to Kota in the north.

items.note: Early scholarly notices of the Udaypur prashasti: Cunningham in the seventh and tenth Survey reports (1874-75, 1876-77); Buhler in Epigraphia Indica vol. 1 (1888).
items.gloss: It was also printed in the seventh and tenth reports (1874-75 and 1876-77) of the Survey by Major General Alexander Cunningham, first head of the Archaeological Survey of India. J. Buhler mentioned it in the first volume of Epigraphia Indica in 1888.

items.note: Udaypur prashasti verse 1 (Hindi translation): invocation of Shambhu with the moon's crescent and serpent garland of Ganga-water.
items.gloss: Om Namah Shivaya. May Shambhu, on whose forehead the crescent of the moon shines like a wish-fulfilling creeper and around whose neck is a serpent garland sprinkled with Ganga water, bring you well-being.

items.note: Verse 2: Shiva before whom heavenly apsaras dance to Nandi's drumming and Narada's song.
items.gloss: With the sound of the (mridanga) played by the intoxicated Nandi's hands and with the charming songs of Narada, the heavenly apsaras always dance before whom, may that Shiva bring you well-being.

items.note: Prashasti verses 5-6: a hero rose from the fire-pit through Vasishtha's power to recover the cow and was told he would be king named Paramara (Agnikula legend).
items.gloss: ... when (he) forcibly took away the cow, then through the influence of (Vasishtha) a hero arose from the fire-pit who alone destroyed the enemy army. Having killed the enemies he brought back the cow; then the sage said: 'You will be a king by the name Paramara.'

items.note: Verse 7: Upendraraja in that lineage.
items.gloss: In that lineage was born Upendraraja, whose fame is sung by the gods and who is like a jewel among the twice-born, and who by his valour has attained the dignity of high kingship.

items.note: Verse 8: his son Vairisimha set up victory pillars with prashastis on the earth.
items.gloss: His son was Vairisimha, who was like a lion to elephant-like kings, strongest among the valiant, and who set up victory pillars with prashastis on the earth bounded by the four seas.

items.note: Prashasti verses 9-10: Siyaka, supreme among victorious kings, and his successor Vakpati.
items.gloss: From him was born Shri Siyaka, whose footstool was coloured by the jewel-radiance of the crowns of the kings of the earth and in whose sword's water-waves enemy hosts drowned, the foremost of victorious kings. From him came Shri Vakpati, who was like the sun to the lotus-eyes of the young women of Avanti, self-radiant with the gleam of the sword in his hand, like Indra, and whose horses drank the waters of the Ganga and the sea.

items.note: Verse 13-14: Vakpatirajadeva praised as learned in rhetoric, poetry, logic and scripture, his feet coloured by crowns of Karnata, Lata, Kerala and Chola kings.
items.gloss: His son, an ornament for the whole earth, sole refuge of virtues, whose wrath grew by wealth taken from enemies conquered in valour, skilled in oratory, high poetry, logic and the scriptures, whose fame is sung by good men by the name of Shrimat Vakpatirajadeva. Whose lotus feet were coloured by the crown jewels of Karnata, Lata, Kerala and Chola kings, and who was known as a wish-fulfilling tree for petitioners.

items.note: Verse 15: he defeated the Yuvaraja and killed his commanders at Tripuri.
items.gloss: Desiring victory at the city of Tripuri, he defeated the Yuvaraja in battle, killed his commanders and raised his sword high.

items.note: Verse 16: Sindhuraja, the younger brother, defeated the Huna king; Bhoja was born to him.
items.gloss: His younger brother Shri Sindhuraja won victory by conquering the Huna king, from whom was born Bhojaraja, who made even excellent men tremble and who was a unique jewel.

items.note: Verses 17-18: Bhoja enjoyed the whole earth from Kailasa to Malaya; the poet-king praised as unmatched.
items.gloss: He who enjoyed the entire earth from Kailasa to Malaya and from the rising mountain to the setting mountain like Prithu, who easily uprooted the guardians of the directions with his bowstring and threw them in the directions, and who gladdened the earth with supreme love. What he achieved, ordained, gave and knew, none else could do. What more praise can there be of Kaviraja Shri Bhoja.

items.note: Verse 19: forces of Chedi, Karnata, Lata, Gurjara kings and Turks defeated merely by Bhoja's servants.
items.gloss: The armies of the Karnata, the lord of Lata, the Gurjara king and the Turks, chiefly the Chedi king Indratha, Togala and Bhima, were conquered by his mere servants, and so the strength of his traditional armies is counted, not that of his warriors (since the warriors had not yet had their turn).

items.note: Verse 20: Bhoja built temples such as Kedareshvara, Rameshvara, Somanatha, Sundira, Kala, Anala and Rudra.
items.gloss: He who built on all sides temples such as Kedareshvara, Rameshvara, Somanatha, Sundira, Kala, Anala and Rudra, and made the sacred earth true to its name.

items.note: Verses 21-22: after Bhoja went to heaven the earth was covered in darkness of enemies; Udayaditya rose like the sun and rescued the earth as the Varaha incarnation did.
items.gloss: After the Shiva-devotee (King Bhoja), whose glory was like the sun, went to heaven, the whole earth, like the city of Dhara, was covered with the darkness of enemies and his traditional warriors grew weak; then Udayadityadeva rose like the sun, destroying the towering darkness of enemies with the rays of his sword and delighting all people. The work of rescuing the earth that the Varaha avatar did, how easily this Paramara did it, how wonderful.

claim.value: prashasti v.21 places Udayaditya after Bhoja's death, no kinship word in the verse

items.note: Calls this the most important of Udaypur's inscriptions and says 11 inscriptions in all are found at Udaypur, telling of the political, economic and social conditions of the period.
items.gloss: Among Udaypur's inscriptions this is the most important, and in this series a total of 11 inscriptions are found from Udaypur, which tell about the political, economic and social conditions of this period.

items.note: Author says the inscriptions have nothing to do with magic or buried treasure, a common village belief; treasure-hunting around old settlements, forts and ruins.
items.gloss: In no way are they connected with sorcery or treasures buried somewhere, as is the common superstition among villagers. Not only villagers but a large section in cities too has had a vulture's eye for buried treasure in any old settlement. Around us you will find many forts, palaces and ruins dug up here and there, where people come in the dark or desolation of night hoping to brighten their fortune. We do not know how successful such attempts to steal something from history are.

items.note: Recommends that translations of inscriptions be displayed at the temple itself, for villagers and tourists, and not on worn tin pieces; questions why read inscriptions are locked in government vaults.
items.gloss: At least, had clean and good translations of these inscriptions been available in the temple complex, they would have helped improve the understanding of the villagers and been useful to visiting tourists for local history. It is strange that when these inscriptions have been read, they are kept locked in government vaults. Whose intention was it that they not be shown to the public outside, and, if by luck they survive somewhere, that a veil be left on them? Why did it never occur to some leader or officer that translations of inscriptions found in temples, palaces and forts should be put up right there, and their presentation should not be on worn tin pieces in a stale way.

items.note: Author says inscriptions should be engraved with care on precious metal or strong stone; Udaypur has enough of them to hold interested visitors a long time.
items.gloss: These are priceless writings of the history around us. They should be inscribed with great care and respect on precious metal or strong stone. In Udaypur there are so many that they are enough to hold interested people for a long time.

items.note: General statement: temples and viharas as religious, educational and social centres; building and managing temples was a public responsibility with the state's role most important.
items.gloss: Since ancient times temples and viharas have been active and prosperous centres not only of religious but of educational and social activities in Indian society. They can also be considered the oldest pivot of our social system. The construction and management of temples has been a matter of public responsibility, in which the state's role was most important.

items.note: Paramara-era Sarasvati Kanthabharana institutions as knowledge centres teaching all subjects; a hostel in-charge Govinda Bhatta at Mandapa Durga (Mandu).
items.gloss: The Sarasvati Kanthabharana built in the Paramara period were excellent knowledge centres of their time, where there was a tradition of teaching all subjects. This tradition of knowledge continued for centuries. Even today documents tell us that a person named Govinda Bhatta was in charge of the hostel attached to the Sarasvati Kanthabharana of Mandapa Durga (present Mandu).

items.note: General temple-economics point: running large institutions needed financial and administrative arrangements; example of Nalanda's revenue from two hundred villages (not Udaypur).
items.gloss: Building huge temples was one task, and the economic and administrative responsibilities of running them as institutions were another important task. For the economic needs of Nalanda University's students and teachers, the revenue of two hundred villages, grain, fruit, flowers and milk were assured. These free grants from the state were used to run and maintain these huge complexes, and a system of officers and staff worked to oversee them.
